paragraphs.text: Vitelliform macular dystrophies (VMD) are inherited retinal dystrophies characterized by yellow, round deposits visible on fundus examination, seen in juvenile Best macular dystrophy and in adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (Manes et al., 2013). VMD caused by mutation in IMPG1, which encodes the SPACR protein of the photoreceptor extracellular (interphotoreceptor) matrix, can be transmitted in an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive fashion; most patients have a normal or moderately decreased electrooculogram Arden ratio (Manes et al., 2013). Onset is usually in adulthood with moderate visual impairment (Meunier et al., 2014), although onset in early childhood has been reported (Brandl et al., 2017).

paragraphs.text: Meunier et al. (2014) reviewed clinical, imaging, and EOG findings in 49 families with vitelliform macular dystrophy without identified mutation in BEST1 or PRPH2. IMPG1 was the causal gene in 3 families (11 patients) and IMPG2 in a fourth family (2 patients). Patients with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations had late onset and moderate visual impairment (mean visual acuity, 20/40; mean age of onset, 42 years), including the sporadic case in IMPG1 family 3 with presumed recessive transmission (age at onset, 38 years; mean visual acuity, 20/50). Drusen-like lesions adjacent to the vitelliform deposits were observed in 9 of 13 patients. The vitelliform material was located above the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) at every stage of the dystrophy, and the RPE was well preserved with classic reflectivity on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT). EOG results were normal or borderline in 9 cases.

paragraphs.text: Brandl et al. (2017) described 2 simplex patients with IMPG1-associated VMD with onset in early childhood. Patient 1, a boy from a German family, was the only affected family member; at age 13 years he had reduced visual acuity (0.2 and 0.1 logMAR in the right and left eyes), and fundus examination showed central RPE abnormalities with foveal detachment. Patient 2, a boy from a consanguineous Turkish family, was diagnosed with VMD at age 2 years and had fluctuating visual acuity of about 0.2 logMAR in both eyes over 8 years of follow-up. At age 10, multifocal ERG was normal and the EOG Arden ratio was borderline to slightly abnormally low. Fundus photographs showed a singular vitelliform lesion in the central macula of both eyes, which increased in area during follow-up; SD-OCT showed a bilateral, central, dome-shaped foveal detachment of the neurosensory retina. The underlying hyperreflective material was reabsorbed, leaving an optically empty cavity, photoreceptor outer segments were elongated, and Bruch membrane and RPE appeared well preserved. Fundus autofluorescence showed circular hyperfluorescence that decreased over time. No satellite drusen were seen. His heterozygous parents, aged 35 and 40 years, were asymptomatic with full visual acuity and normal multimodal retinal imaging.

paragraphs.text: In a large family with autosomal dominant VMD, Manes et al. (2013) used gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.713T-G transversion in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution; the same mutation was found in 2 other families with autosomal dominant VMD. Structural modeling indicated that the L238R substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of SPACR, the protein encoded by IMPG1. Screening of 144 probands with various forms of macular dystrophy revealed 3 other IMPG1 mutations: 2 individuals from a family with autosomal recessive VMD were homozygous for a splice site mutation (c.807+1G-T), and 2 individuals from another family were compound heterozygous for c.461T-C (L154P) and c.1519C-T (R507X) mutations.

paragraphs.text: By next-generation sequencing of IMPG1 and IMPG2 in 106 VMD patients negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations, Brandl et al. (2017) identified 2 IMPG1 mutations in 2 simplex patients with early childhood onset. Patient 1, from a German family, carried a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution in the SEA I domain, predicted pathogenic by 3 in silico algorithms; parental data were not available. Patient 2, from a consanguineous Turkish family, was homozygous for a c.807+5G-A splice site mutation in intron 7; homozygosity was confirmed by segregation analysis in the parents. In a minigene assay in HEK293 cells, the mutation caused skipping of exon 7 in about half of the transcripts.

paragraphs.text: Olivier et al. (2021) identified an IMPG1 splice variant by exome sequencing in a family with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and found the same variant in individuals from 2 families with either RP or VMD. Screening of 596 RP and VMD families identified 8 additional families with different missense or nonsense IMPG1 variants. Morpholino-mediated knockdown of Impg1 and its paralog Impg2 in medaka fish produced a phenotype including decreased length of rod and cone photoreceptor outer segments. The authors concluded that monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants are associated with RP.

paragraphs.text: In a large family with autosomal dominant vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD4), Manes et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.713T-G transversion in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution, by gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing. The mutation was subsequently found in 2 other families with autosomal dominant VMD and the same phenotype. Structural modeling indicated that the substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of SPACR.

paragraphs.text: In a German boy with VMD4 who was the only affected member of his family, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7 of the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution in the SEA I domain. The variant was predicted to be pathogenic by 3 in silico algorithms; parental genetic data were not available. At age 13 years the patient had reduced visual acuity and central RPE abnormalities with foveal detachment.

agent.process_note: I read all 5 papers. Four were available only as abstracts (Manes 2013, Meunier 2014, Gupta 2021, Olivier 2021). Brandl 2017 was full text, and I read all of it. I used Grep to check ages, ancestry and consanguinity in Brandl. No reference data were supplied, so the intro gives no IMPG1 MIM number or chromosome location. No mapped locus is given in the abstracts, so there is no mapping section. Brandl's text gives inconsistent ages for its IMPG1 patients, both in the text and in its Table 2. It also describes L238P once as a T-to-G change but as c.713T>C in its results and table. I used c.713T>C and avoided the conflicting ages. Olivier 2021 concerns retinitis pigmentosa and gives no variant names. I mention it only under genotype/phenotype correlations.
